title: Towards AI Agents for Course Instruction in Higher Education: Early Experiences from the Field
extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI-based instructor agent can be designed, deployed, and evaluated as the primary instructional interface in a real higher-education classroom. The authors argue that, while LLMs are increasingly discussed as educational tools, there is limited evidence on how to integrate them into authentic live teaching settings, especially in higher education. The study therefore focuses on an in-the-wild implementation of an AI Instructor Agent and an accompanying analytics framework for understanding student engagement during classroom use.

The intervention was an LLM-driven Instructor Agent built in Microsoft Teams Copilot and integrated into a graduate-level Introduction to Cloud Computing course workflow at the Indian Institute of Science. In each 90-minute lecture, the human instructor briefly introduced the weekly topic, students then interacted with the AI agent on laptops during class to explore concepts, clarify doubts, and attempt non-graded quizzes, after which they submitted chat transcripts for automated evaluation. The broader workflow also included small-group peer discussion, instructor-led Q&A, TA-led tutorial/lab sessions, and periodic proctored quizzes. To assess engagement, the authors developed an automated transcript-analysis framework that measured topic coverage, topic depth, and turn length.

The population consisted of 17 enrolled students in one course cohort, spanning senior undergraduate, Master's, and PhD students at a single Indian institution. The context was a real in-person higher-education classroom in a 4-credit cloud computing course during the August/Fall 2025 semester, with supporting digital infrastructure including Moodle, Microsoft Copilot, and cloud-based function workflows. Human instructors and TAs remained involved in curriculum design, topic introduction, tutorials, and formal assessment, while the AI agent handled much of the concept-level instructional interaction.

The paper concludes that structured integration of an AI instructor agent is feasible in a live classroom and can support inquiry-driven, reflective learning. Preliminary findings across two instructional modules suggested that student interactions evolved from broader topic exploration toward deeper, more focused inquiry, with lower topic coverage but greater topic depth and somewhat longer responses over time. At the same time, the authors stress that these are early findings and not yet evidence of improved learning outcomes; they note challenges including hallucinated references, difficulty generating useful figures, uncertainty about expected topic depth, and limits to generalizability from a small single-course deployment. They propose future work linking engagement metrics to graded performance and incorporating more capable agentic AI workflows.

identified_tools.name: Microsoft Copilot
identified_tools.description: Microsoft Copilot is a conversational AI platform used to configure and deploy LLM-based agents with persistent prompts, course materials, and guardrails.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper designed and deployed an AI Instructor Agent within Microsoft Teams Copilot as the primary in-class instructor for a graduate cloud computing course, with students interacting via chat during live class sessions.

findings.finding_summary: Across two successive instructional weeks in a graduate cloud computing course, median topic coverage decreased from 52.5% to 31.0%, while average topic depth increased from 1.33 to 2.06 and average turn length per topic increased from 48.2 to 54.4 words. The authors interpret this as a shift from broad exploration to more focused, deeper inquiry during AI-mediated instruction, but no direct learning outcome or graded achievement result is reported. Sample comprised 17 officially enrolled students in the course.
findings.measure: Engagement analytics from student–agent chat transcripts: topic coverage (%), average topic depth (0–3 ordinal scale), and average turn length per topic (words)
findings.effect_size: Coverage: 52.5% to 31.0%; Depth: 1.33 to 2.06; Turn length: 48.2 to 54.4 words

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: ChatGPT is OpenAI's family of GPT-based large language models used for natural-language interaction and text analysis.
identified_tools.use_case: An OpenAI GPT 4o-mini endpoint was used as the evaluation engine to analyze student chat transcripts, generate engagement metrics, create plots, and produce personalized PDF feedback reports.

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports that the GPT-based evaluation workflow automatically processed uploaded transcripts, generated structured engagement reports, plots, and PDF feedback without human intervention. This was presented as enabling standardized, scalable, and privacy-preserving evaluation, but no quantitative efficiency metric, accuracy benchmark, or effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Automation and standardization of transcript evaluation workflow

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Gemini is Google's family of large language models and conversational AI tools.
identified_tools.use_case: Gemini was used during course curriculum development through instructor conversations to help iteratively design course content; it was also mentioned as an alternative model some students preferred, but it was not the deployed classroom instructor agent in this study.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an early field deployment with preliminary observational analysis of transcript-derived engagement metrics in one course cohort, not an RCT or strong quasi-experiment. The paper explicitly notes that more detailed empirical results are pending and does not report validated learning outcome impacts.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows suggestive positive changes in engagement patterns, but impact on actual learning outcomes is unclear because no assessment gains, effect sizes, or causal comparisons are reported.
